lead: Today Hebrews names the source of Christ's priesthood: not family descent but “the power of an indestructible life”, the life of the Risen One. Luke shows Jesus on his way to Jerusalem, where that life will pass through death, and someone asks him how many will be saved. He answers with a call: strive to enter through the narrow door. The key words are indestructible, approach and strive.

r.h: The power of an indestructible life
set: In 7:1–10 the writer has shown that Melchizedek, who blessed Abraham and received a tenth from him, stands above the priesthood of Levi. Now he draws the conclusion. Under the law of Moses the priests came from the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron. Jesus was of the tribe of Judah. If he is a priest, his priesthood must rest on something other than descent.
The writer speaks with deep respect of Israel's worship. His point is that God himself, in Psalm 110:4, had promised another priest, so the old order was always pointing beyond itself.
str: vv. 11–12: if the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, no other priest would be needed.
vv. 13–14: our Lord came from Judah.
vv. 15–17: a priest by the power of an indestructible life.
vv. 18–19: a better hope, through which we approach God.
kw: Literally “that cannot be dissolved”. The life of the risen Christ is beyond the reach of death. This is the ground of his priesthood: “he always lives to make intercession” (7:25).
A legal word for cancelling an arrangement. Hebrews applies it to the rule that only descendants of Aaron could be priests, now that Christ has come.
The verb of worship. The whole purpose of priesthood is to let people come near to God, and in Christ this happens fully.
vv: For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah,
Hebrews takes for granted what the Gospels tell: Jesus was of the house of David, of the tribe of Judah (Matthew 1:1–3; Luke 1:27).
but through the power of an indestructible life.

Aaron's priesthood passed from father to son because every priest died. Christ's priesthood passes to no successor, because he lives for ever. Priests of the Church act in his person, not as his successors.
(for the law made nothing perfect); there is, on the other hand, the introduction of a better hope, through which we approach God.
The law was holy and good (Romans 7:12), but it could not by itself bring people to the goal. The “better hope” is Christ himself, the one through whom we draw near.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Old Law is holy, spiritual and good, yet still imperfect, a first stage on the way to the Kingdom (CCC 1963). It also says that Christ is the one true Priest and that the ministerial priesthood makes his one priesthood present, quoting St Thomas Aquinas: only Christ is the true priest, the others being his ministers (CCC 1545). When a priest of our Church stands at the altar, it is Christ, alive for ever, who offers.

r.h: Strive to enter through the narrow door
set: Since 9:51 Luke has shown Jesus making his way to Jerusalem. Verse 22 reminds the reader of this journey: everything Jesus teaches along the road is said on the way to the Cross.
The question “will only a few be saved?” was discussed by teachers of the time. Jesus does not give a number. He turns a question about others into a call to the one who asked.
str: vv. 22–23: the journey and the question.
v. 24: strive to enter through the narrow door.
vv. 25–27: the shut door and the knocking from outside.
vv. 28–30: the banquet of the kingdom, with guests from every direction.
kw: From the word for an athletic contest, the root of our word “agony”. Entering the kingdom takes the whole of a person.
A door, not a road: there is a moment to go in. Jesus speaks of himself as the door elsewhere (John 10:9).
I do not know where you come from
The householder does not deny having seen them. He denies any real belonging, any bond of life with them.
vv: Lord, will only a few be saved?
A question of curiosity. Jesus does not answer the question of how many; he answers the question of how.
Strive to enter through the narrow door;
The door is open now. The effort asked is not to earn entry but to go in while the door stands open, by grace.
We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.
Being near Jesus is not the same as following him. Christians who eat at his table every Sunday hear this as a word to themselves.
Then people will come from east and west, from north and south, and will eat in the kingdom of God.
The prophets foresaw the nations gathering at God's feast (Isaiah 25:6). The table is wide, and Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are already at it.
ch: This warning is addressed to those who heard Jesus in person, and through them to every disciple; it is not a judgement on any people. The Catechism takes up the Lord's call to “enter by the narrow gate” (Matthew 7:13–14) in its teaching on the last things, as an urgent call to conversion and responsibility (CCC 1036). The good news is in verse 29: the door is narrow, but the hall is full.

study: Christ's priesthood rests on “an indestructible life”. How does the Resurrection change the way I pray at the Holy Qurbono?
Do I ask questions about others' salvation more readily than I strive for my own? What would striving look like for me this week?
